quiz.q: What does it mean that iterator adapters like `map` and `filter` are 'lazy'?
options: They only describe work and do nothing until a consumer runs the chain
quiz.explain: Adapters build a plan but touch no items until a consumer (collect, sum, for, ...) pulls values through.

quiz.q: Which of these actually runs an iterator chain?
quiz.explain: collect is a consumer — it drives the chain and gathers results. map, filter, and rev are lazy adapters that only describe work.

quiz.q: What is the difference between `.iter()` and `.into_iter()` on a Vec?
options: iter() borrows each item; into_iter() takes ownership and consumes the Vec
iter() is faster but less safe
quiz.explain: iter() yields &T (borrows), leaving the Vec usable. into_iter() yields owned T and consumes the collection.

quiz.q: Why does `let v = nums.iter().map(|n| n * 2);` (with no consumer) not double anything?
options: Adapters are lazy — without a consumer, no work runs
You must use a for loop instead of map
quiz.explain: map is a lazy adapter; it just builds a plan. Add a consumer like .collect() or .sum() to actually run it.

flashcards.back: Adapters (map, filter) only describe work. Nothing runs until a consumer (collect, sum, count, for) pulls items through the chain.
collect (into a collection), sum, count, for loops. They finish the chain and produce a value or side effect.
iter() borrows (&T), iter_mut() borrows mutably (&mut T) to edit in place, into_iter() takes ownership (T) and consumes the collection.

flashcards.front: Why does collect() sometimes need a type annotation?
flashcards.back: collect can build many kinds of collection, so the compiler needs to know which: e.g. `let v: Vec<i32> = it.collect();`.
